units.title: Foundations: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, the DOM, fetch, and tooling
units.intro: Weeks 3 to 9 built a page by hand: the document, its stylesheet, the JavaScript that reads and changes it, the events it answers, the data it fetches, and the modules it is split into. These topics are that material in CS300 Practice: each idea is a short step you edit, run, and check, with the console or the page showing what your code did. Nothing here is required this term. Use it to revisit an idea before a React week leans on it, to see in Why React behaves this way which JavaScript rule is behind a React behavior that surprised you, or to meet Node, npm, and Vite in Tooling from scratch before the Week 10 project. Take a topic in the order listed, because each one assumes the ones before it.
localNotes: Every step here can also be downloaded and run from a folder on your own computer; the HTML, CSS, and DOM steps open as plain pages, and the tooling topic's last step walks through npm install and npm run dev.

units.title: Git and GitHub: version control, pull requests, and deployment
units.intro: We covered Git in class: commits, branches, merges, and working with a repository on GitHub. These topics are practice for that material, at your own pace and in any week. Git basics keeps a project's history on your own computer, and Git collaboration takes it to GitHub, where you resolve a conflict, open a pull request, and merge it the way a team does. Deploy with GitHub Pages is where your own project goes on the web: by its last step, a React project of yours has an address anyone can open, and every push updates it.
localNotes: Git runs in a terminal on your own computer, not in this site, so the steps that say "on your computer" need Git installed, and the GitHub steps need a free GitHub account.

units.title: React, Vite, JSX, components, props, and lists
units.intro: In Week 8 we built CourseHub by hand: we wrote the HTML, styled it, and then kept the page in step with our data by finding elements, building strings of markup, and replacing what was on the screen every time something changed. This week you will build the same kind of page with React. You will describe what the page should look like for the data you have, and React will update the DOM for you. You will see how a Vite project is put together, write JSX, split a page into components that receive props, and render lists of data with stable keys, then load that data from a real API. Start with Using CS300 Practice, a fifteen-minute tour of the site; after it, each topic runs in the browser, so you can edit the code, run it, watch the inspector draw your components, and check your work as you go.
localNotes: The Vite scaffold and build steps run on your own computer: you create the project with npm and run npm run build in your own terminal, and CS300 Practice shows the exact commands and the output to expect.

units.title: State, events, and component communication
units.intro: In Week 10 we built the product page: a list of cards rendered from data, split into components that receive props. It could show data but not respond to it, because nothing on the page could change. This week the page comes alive. You will handle a click with an event handler, give a component a value it owns with useState, and watch React re-render only the component whose state changed. Then you will meet the problem every real app runs into, two components that need the same value, and solve it the way React does: move the state up to the parent, pass the value down as a prop, and pass a function down so that a child can ask for a change. In Session 1 we draw that sequence on the board as event, callback prop, setter, and re-render; in CS300 Practice the inspector's flow view draws it for you from the clicks you make, so you can check your mental model against what React really did. In Session 2 the same rule reaches the form fields: React owns what the shopper types, validates it on every keystroke, and adds the new product to the list without changing the array it already holds, which is the one bug this week that produces no error anywhere.
localNotes: Everything this week runs in the browser. If you want to keep working on your own computer, download a step's workspace and run it with npm install and npm run dev, as you did in Vite project anatomy.

units.title: Effects, fetching, persistence, and routing
units.intro: In Week 11 every change on the page came from a click: an event, a setter, a re-render. This week the page starts talking to things outside React, and the two core topics are Effects and Refs and browser APIs. An effect is how a component synchronizes with something that is not a prop or state, such as the document title, a timer, a browser event, or a server, and cleans up after itself; a ref is how it reaches a DOM element or keeps a value across renders without re-rendering. The three follow-through topics apply effects to the three jobs every app has: Persistence keeps a value in localStorage across reloads, Fetching and request states loads data with one status value, cleans up a request that is no longer wanted, and shows you a stale response and a duplicate request in the network pane before fixing them, and Routing turns one page into several with React Router. Work through the first two before the rest, and keep the network view of the CS300 Practice inspector open on every fetching step.
localNotes: Every fetching step also runs against a real server: choose the DummyJSON preset or type your own server's base URL in the API source selector. A routing step's downloaded workspace keeps the real react-router from npm, so npm install and npm run dev give you the browser's own address bar for the walk in the last topic.

units.title: Route data, custom hooks, and URL state
units.intro: Week 12 gave the shop its pages and its requests. This week they meet: each route owns the request for its own data, keyed on the id that useParams reads from the address, and the request logic lives in a custom hook that every page shares. In Route data and custom hooks you reuse useFetch on a list page and a detail page, tell a product the server no longer has from a request that failed, write a useLocalStorage hook that remembers saved products, and read how custom hooks relate to useState and useEffect. In URL state you move a search and a category filter into the address with useSearchParams, so that a shopper can bookmark, share, and press Back through them, show the shareable address with a copy button, and then walk the whole app from the address bar the way the Week 13 integration check asks: direct load, refresh, Back, Forward, and a bad id. Both topics run in CS300 Practice up to that last walk, which is for your own browser.
localNotes: The integration walk in the last step is meant for your own browser: download the URL state workspace, run npm install and npm run dev, and type each address into the address bar, including a refresh on a product page.

units.title: Capstone release check and deployment
units.intro: Week 13 joined the shop's pages and requests and walked the whole app from the address bar. This week is a light one, with the Thanksgiving closure from Thursday, November 26, so both topics are optional, and each fits in one sitting. In Capstone release check you build a small app put together the way the Capstone starter is, preview the build, open every route from a typed address, make the loading, error, and empty states appear on purpose with the boundary data files, and run the tests from a clean install; along the way two bugs turn up that clicking through the app never shows. Deploy with GitHub Pages, from the Git and GitHub unit, puts a React project on the web with the same kind of workflow your Capstone starter carries; it is listed here again so that you can deploy your Capstone early and find a deep-link problem while there is still time to fix it. Do the release check first, then run it again on your own Capstone and keep the record for its verification cases.
localNotes: Both topics run on your own computer, not in this site: the release check needs Node 24, a terminal, and Chrome's DevTools, and the deployment needs Git and a free GitHub account. Every release check step offers a download of the project as that step starts, so you can begin at any step.

units.title: Testing, accessibility, and explaining your code
units.intro: Week 14 checked a release candidate by hand. This week turns those checks into evidence you can show in the Capstone defense. In Testing React components you add Vitest and Testing Library to a project, the same setup your Capstone starter already has, and write a render test, a test that types like a user, and a test of a request that fails, watching each one fail for the right reason before it passes. In Accessibility checks you fix, in the browser, the four problems a routed app most often ships with: a control with no label, focus left behind after a route change, a skipped heading level, and link text that means nothing on its own; then you walk a page by keyboard and run Lighthouse. In Explaining your own code you read a small recipe app you have not seen before and answer the questions the defense asks about it: where each piece of state lives, what each effect depends on, which route renders what, and which tests a change affects. Take the topics in that order; the last one ends with a rehearsal script for your own Capstone.
localNotes: Testing React components runs on your own computer, because Vitest, jsdom, and Testing Library are installed with npm; each step shows the commands and the output to expect, and its download is the project as that step starts. Accessibility checks runs in the browser up to its last step, which uses Lighthouse in Chrome's DevTools on your own Capstone.
